displayed_question.problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluates to zero due to symmetry?

- ${\int }_{-2}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-3}^{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-2}^{4}4\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x$

mathematical_evidence.I: Integral of sin²(x) from -2 to 2 is 2 - sin(4)/2 > 0.
mathematical_evidence.II: tan(2x) has poles at -3π/4, -π/4, π/4, 3π/4 inside (-3,3). On each continuous branch F(x) = -½ ln|cos(2x)|; F tends to +∞ at a pole. The left and right one-sided improper integrals diverge with opposite signs, so their ordinary sum is undefined. Odd symmetry does not cancel independently divergent one-sided integrals.
mathematical_evidence.III: 4 tan(x) has poles at -π/2 and π/2 inside (-2,4). Its antiderivative on continuous branches is -4 ln|cos(x)|, with divergent one-sided improper integrals. Its limits are also asymmetric.
mathematical_evidence.principal_value: A symmetric principal-value regularization gives II zero; neither the prompt nor saved tutorial/example declares this convention. This cannot justify submitting the proposed choice as a confident ordinary-integral answer.
